podcast.body: During the 1962 UK tour, after initially being restricted to only acting as a compere due to work permit issues, Gene Vincent eventually performed this song from off-stage. "Later on he would sing B. Bappelula from off stage as well."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.body: This song, initially released as the B-side to "Woman Love," became Gene Vincent's most memorable hit of the 1950s. Its title has multiple origin stories, including being inspired by the 1920s vaudeville song "Don't Ring Lulu" (per Donald Graves), a "Little Lulu" comic book (per Tex Davis, who is credited as co-writer but widely believed not to have contributed to the writing), or most likely Helen Humes' song "Be-Baba-Leba," later re-recorded by Lionel Hampton as "Hey Baba Reba." Lyrically, it's described as "absolute nonsense" and "gibberish," but its sound was pivotal, being the "precise midpoint" between Elvis Presley's "Heartbreak Hotel" and Little Richard's "Tutti Frutti," and is said to epitomize 1956. During its recording, drummer Dickie Harrell famously let out a scream mid-song so his mother would know he was on the record, a take that was ultimately used. "Be-Bop-A-Lula is by any standards, a quite astonishing record."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
